analysis.one_liner: Directs federal safety agencies to study workplace violence and issue voluntary prevention guidance for employers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered a federal study of workplace violence, then required the Labor Department to publish voluntary, nonbinding advice on how different workplaces — grocery stores, hospitals, restaurants, schools — could reduce the risk of violence to their workers. It would have created no new rules and no penalties. It was referred to committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, workers in jobs with frequent contact with the public — retail clerks, grocery and restaurant staff, hospital and nursing staff, transit and school employees — would have gained a federal playbook of violence-prevention measures: better lighting and sightlines, secured entries, shatter-resistant glass, panic alarms, adequate staffing, security personnel, and de-escalation training. The guidance would have been voluntary, so its practical effect would have depended on employers choosing to adopt it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defined workplace violence broadly — including threats and incidents with no physical injury — so the guidance would have covered the fear and stress that precede actual harm, not just completed attacks.

It required the guidance to be tailored to specific settings, listing grocery stores, retail stores, hospitals, restaurants and bars, schools, and child care centers among them, and to cover both physical fixes (locks, weapon detectors, cameras, alarms) and staffing practices like adequate staff numbers and security guards.
The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health would have studied the problem first and reported recommendations within 15 months, giving the eventual guidance an evidence base.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in the covered industries would have borne the cost of whatever prevention measures they chose to adopt, since the guidance was nonmandatory and the bill created no funding or mandate. Taxpayers would have paid for the federal study. Because the guidance was nonbinding, no one would have been legally required to change anything.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, voluntarily; taxpayers fund the study

drawbacks.text: The guidance would have been explicitly nonmandatory, so nothing in the bill would have forced any employer to actually install the barriers, alarms, staffing levels, or training it describes — a weak tool for a serious safety problem.
The timeline was slow: a study, a report within 15 months, and guidance only within four years of enactment, meaning workers would have waited years for even voluntary advice.

Even voluntary federal guidance can become a reference point in lawsuits and insurance disputes, so some employers would have faced pressure to follow it — a cost an honest supporter should acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to workers is real — workplace violence is a documented hazard in retail, health care, and food service — but the bill's design was deliberately modest: study first, then advice employers could ignore. The costs were correspondingly small. As a first step toward a workplace violence standard it was low-risk; as a safety measure on its own it changed little.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the Safe Workplaces Act on June 7, 2024, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the bill's entire recorded history is the introduction and the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in retail, health care, restaurants, and other public-facing industries are better off, because even voluntary federal guidance — which can raise expectations and be cited in disputes — never materialized. No workplace violence study or guidance will be produced, so the status quo remains.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided even voluntary guidance

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing OSHA to issue voluntary workplace violence prevention guidance.

for.name: Reps. Nikema Williams, Hank Johnson, and Adam Smith
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill had no other cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — and it died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee never moved the bill; no Republican supported it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have published voluntary violence-prevention guidance aimed squarely at these workplaces, covering barriers, cameras, alarms, staffing levels, and training. Because it was nonmandatory, the direct cost was optional, but guidance of this kind tends to raise expectations and can surface in liability and insurance disputes.

Health care settings were explicitly listed as a workplace type for the tailored guidance, and patient-on-staff violence is a known hazard there. The guidance would have been voluntary, so compliance would have been a choice.

industries.industry: Occupational safety research and consulting (NIOSH, safety consultants)
industries.note: A mandated federal study and new guidance would have generated research activity and demand for prevention consulting and training services.
